required_units.text: Space for your own cycle or review record, questions and notes, followed by your treatment card.
Gemcitabine + cisplatin · 28-day scheduleNational Cancer Control Programme (NCCP) 00282

Record each cycle separately. Each medicine has its own symptom table. Mark the worst symptoms since your last review, when they occurred and what they stopped you doing. Overlapping symptoms can be recorded under more than one medicine; you do not have to identify the cause.

These are patient-language severity prompts, not a validated questionnaire or a formal Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) grading tool. Your team assigns the clinical grade. Serious symptoms override the columns: call without waiting to decide a severity level.
Use a new record sheet for each cycle or review. Copy or print another sheet when needed; the number of sheets does not prescribe the length of treatment.
Source-reconciled feasibility draft; independent clinician, pharmacy and patient review pending.
Bring this record to every treatment and review; your team confirms the dose and next appointment.
Days 1, 8 and 15 · every 28 days · copy this sheet for another cycle of the same phase.

unique_source_inventory.text: Severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain: call emergency services. Do not wait for an online answer.

Temperature 37.5°C or higher, 36°C or lower, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell — even with a normal temperature. Call oncology immediately for fever, shaking chills, suddenly feeling unwell, unusual bleeding, new breathlessness, very little urine, severe rash or vomiting that prevents drinking. Follow your hospital’s temperature and contact instructions. Severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, collapse or seizures: call 112/999.

Follow the urgent contact instructions from your treating hospital. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Outside clinic hours, use your instructed out-of-hours pathway or the emergency department.
This page does not diagnose symptoms or decide whether it is safe to stay at home. You do not need to know which medicine caused a symptom before calling.
Help control advanced urothelial cancer and its symptoms.
Gemcitabine interferes with making DNA, which dividing cancer cells need. Healthy blood-forming cells and other tissues can also be affected.
What to watch forReport fever, unusual bleeding, breathlessness, rash, swelling or reduced urine promptly.

Cisplatin forms links in DNA that interfere with copying and repair. This helps stop cancer cells dividing, but healthy tissues may also be affected. Kidney protection with fluids and monitoring is central to cisplatin treatment.
What to watch forReport ringing in the ears, hearing changes, numbness or loss of function. Tell the team if you cannot drink, are passing less urine or become swollen or breathless during fluids.
The drawings are simplified explanations of drug action, not anatomical pictures or a prediction of response.
This shows treatment timing, not guaranteed symptom-free days. Your team confirms the active phase and dates.

Gemcitabine is given on days 1, 8 and 15. Cisplatin is usually given after gemcitabine on day 1; the source also permits day 2. The cycle repeats every 28 days, usually for four to six cycles. Your unit confirms your actual cisplatin day and appointments.
This is NCCP 00282: cisplatin 70 mg/m² with gemcitabine days 1, 8 and 15 over 28 days. It is distinct from split-dose cisplatin and four-cycle upper-tract adjuvant treatment.
Safety testing and cancer-response assessment have different purposes. Your plan may change after illness or a dose adjustment.

A randomised trial in previously untreated advanced urothelial cancer compared 28-day gemcitabine/cisplatin with MVAC. Response rates were 49% and 46%; overall survival did not differ significantly (hazard ratio 1.04, 95% confidence interval 0.82–1.32).
The study did not prove every GemCis schedule equivalent. It used cisplatin on day 2 and predates newer systemic options. Group averages cannot predict an individual outcome.

Timing and directions
Day 1Take one capsule one hour prior to chemotherapy; bring it to the day ward.
Days 2-3Take one capsule daily for two days starting the day after chemotherapy.
Days 2-4Take once daily for three days starting the day after chemotherapy.
Days 1-4Take one capsule daily for four days starting on the day of chemotherapy.
100,000 units/mL, 1 mL PO QDS
Continuous during chemotherapyRinse 1 mL around the mouth four times daily after meals during the chemotherapy regimen.

Continuous during chemotherapyRinse 10 mL around the mouth for at least 1 minute four times daily; expel after rinsing.
As required during chemotherapyTake one tablet three times daily as required.
4 mg STAT, then 2 mg PO QDS PRN

unique_source_inventory.text: Severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain: call emergency services. Do not wait for an online answer.

Temperature 37.5°C or higher, 36°C or lower, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell — even with a normal temperature. Call oncology immediately for fever, shaking chills, suddenly feeling unwell, unusual bleeding, new breathlessness, very little urine, severe rash or vomiting that prevents drinking. Follow your hospital’s temperature and contact instructions. Severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, collapse or seizures: call 112/999.

Follow the urgent contact instructions from your treating hospital. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Outside clinic hours, use your instructed out-of-hours pathway or the emergency department.
This page does not diagnose symptoms or decide whether it is safe to stay at home. You do not need to know which medicine caused a symptom before calling.
Help control advanced urothelial cancer in patients fit for this intensive combination.

Methotrexate interferes with folate-dependent reactions that cells need to make DNA. This can slow cancer-cell division, while also affecting blood-cell production and the lining of the mouth and bowel.

What to watch forTell the pharmacist about all painkillers, antibiotics, supplements and other medicines because interactions can increase methotrexate toxicity. Report new cough or breathlessness, mouth ulcers, unusual bleeding, jaundice, reduced urine or severe rash promptly.
Vinblastine prevents cells from separating normally when they divide. It can also affect blood cells, nerves and bowel movement.
What to watch forReport constipation, abdominal swelling, numbness or pain around the drip.
Doxorubicin interacts with DNA and topoisomerase II, disrupting copying and repair. Its heart and tissue effects require particular care.

What to watch forFollow the unit’s cisplatin hydration plan and individual fluid target. The source advises 2–3 litres on Day 1 to reduce bladder irritation from cyclophosphamide; the team must adapt this if heart or kidney problems restrict fluids. Report blood in urine or painful urination promptly.

Cisplatin forms links in DNA that interfere with copying and repair. This helps stop cancer cells dividing, but healthy tissues may also be affected. Kidney protection with fluids and monitoring is central to cisplatin treatment.
What to watch forReport ringing in the ears, hearing changes, numbness or loss of function. Tell the team if you cannot drink, are passing less urine or become swollen or breathless during fluids.
The drawings are simplified explanations of drug action, not anatomical pictures or a prediction of response.
This shows treatment timing, not guaranteed symptom-free days. Your team confirms the active phase and dates.

Methotrexate is given on day 1; vinblastine, doxorubicin and cisplatin on day 2. The cycle repeats every 14 days. Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) is prescribed on days 3–7. The consultant sets total treatment duration; no fixed four- or six-cycle course is implied.
This is the 14-day MVAC schedule with G-CSF. It must not be confused with 28-day MVAC or three-drug CMV.
Safety testing and cancer-response assessment have different purposes. Your plan may change after illness or a dose adjustment.
Check infection-fighting cells, haemoglobin and platelets.
Check safe drug handling and detect organ effects.
Assess cancer control separately from safety blood tests.
Detect cisplatin electrolyte, hearing and nerve effects.

Full blood count, kidney and liver tests, ECG, review of hearing, nerves, bowel function, medicines and any fluid collections. Hearing testing is arranged when indicated. Doxorubicin schedules need cardiac assessment and echocardiogram/MUGA if over 65 or clinically indicated, with lifetime anthracycline exposure reviewed.
Full blood count, kidney and liver tests before each cycle; review symptoms, infection, bowel function, hearing, nerves and fluid balance. Review cardiac symptoms and cumulative doxorubicin exposure.
Extra tests may be needed for symptoms, infection or abnormal results.
Follow abnormal results and ongoing symptoms until a plan is agreed.

Confirm each treatment day, blood-test appointments, support medicines and any growth-factor or folinic-acid prescription.

Treatment is given intravenously. Methotrexate and vinblastine are short administrations; where used, doxorubicin is given through carefully checked access. Cisplatin requires prescribed hydration and a longer visit. The team confirms exact administration and observation times.

Use one written anti-sickness plan, including medicines before treatment, tablets for home and rescue treatment. Your team reconciles steroids, interactions and any stomach-protection medicine from your local prescription. Cisplatin needs prescribed intravenous fluids and electrolyte monitoring/replacement. Follow your own fluid advice; tell the team about heart failure or fluid restriction. Review kidney function, hearing, nerves and other medicines before treatment. Methotrexate interacts with several medicines, including some antibiotics, anti-inflammatory painkillers and proton-pump inhibitors. Do not start, stop or combine medicines without oncology/pharmacy advice. The aprepitant–vinblastine interaction also requires pharmacy reconciliation. G-CSF on days 3–7 supports white-cell recovery; report fever even when receiving it.
Review lasting effects, support needs and any line/pump removal.

In 263 patients with advanced urothelial cancer, dose-dense MVAC with G-CSF was compared with conventional MVAC. Complete responses were 21% versus 9%; median progression-free survival was 9.1 versus 8.2 months (hazard ratio 0.75, 95% confidence interval 0.58–0.98).

The initial report did not show a statistically significant overall-survival difference. These advanced-disease findings do not establish the benefit of a perioperative course. A response is not the same as cure.

CMV · before definitive bladder treatmentNational Cancer Control Programme (NCCP) 00337

Record each cycle separately. Each medicine has its own symptom table. Mark the worst symptoms since your last review, when they occurred and what they stopped you doing. Overlapping symptoms can be recorded under more than one medicine; you do not have to identify the cause.

These are patient-language severity prompts, not a validated questionnaire or a formal Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) grading tool. Your team assigns the clinical grade. Serious symptoms override the columns: call without waiting to decide a severity level.
Use a new record sheet for each cycle or review. Copy or print another sheet when needed; the number of sheets does not prescribe the length of treatment.
Source-reconciled feasibility draft; independent clinician, pharmacy and patient review pending.
Bring this record to every treatment and review; your team confirms the dose and next appointment.

unique_source_inventory.text: Severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain: call emergency services. Do not wait for an online answer.

Temperature 37.5°C or higher, 36°C or lower, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell — even with a normal temperature. Call oncology immediately for fever, shaking chills, suddenly feeling unwell, unusual bleeding, new breathlessness, very little urine, severe rash or vomiting that prevents drinking. Follow your hospital’s temperature and contact instructions. Severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, collapse or seizures: call 112/999.

Follow the urgent contact instructions from your treating hospital. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Outside clinic hours, use your instructed out-of-hours pathway or the emergency department.
This page does not diagnose symptoms or decide whether it is safe to stay at home. You do not need to know which medicine caused a symptom before calling.
Treat possible microscopic spread before definitive local treatment for muscle-invasive bladder cancer.

Methotrexate interferes with folate-dependent reactions that cells need to make DNA. This can slow cancer-cell division, while also affecting blood-cell production and the lining of the mouth and bowel.

What to watch forTell the pharmacist about all painkillers, antibiotics, supplements and other medicines because interactions can increase methotrexate toxicity. Report new cough or breathlessness, mouth ulcers, unusual bleeding, jaundice, reduced urine or severe rash promptly.
Vinblastine prevents cells from separating normally when they divide. It can also affect blood cells, nerves and bowel movement.
What to watch forReport constipation, abdominal swelling, numbness or pain around the drip.

Cisplatin forms links in DNA that interfere with copying and repair. This helps stop cancer cells dividing, but healthy tissues may also be affected. Kidney protection with fluids and monitoring is central to cisplatin treatment.
What to watch forReport ringing in the ears, hearing changes, numbness or loss of function. Tell the team if you cannot drink, are passing less urine or become swollen or breathless during fluids.

Folinic acid 15 mg is prescribed every six hours for four doses, starting 24 hours after each methotrexate dose (days 2 and 9). Confirm the written prescription.
The NCCP body specifies 21-day CMV; a 14-day footer label conflicts with it. The prescribing team must reconcile that source error. This schedule has no doxorubicin and requires folinic-acid rescue.

unique_source_inventory.text: Severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain: call emergency services. Do not wait for an online answer.

Temperature 37.5°C or higher, 36°C or lower, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell — even with a normal temperature. Call oncology immediately for fever, shaking chills, suddenly feeling unwell, unusual bleeding, new breathlessness, very little urine, severe rash or vomiting that prevents drinking. Follow your hospital’s temperature and contact instructions. Severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, collapse or seizures: call 112/999.

Follow the urgent contact instructions from your treating hospital. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Outside clinic hours, use your instructed out-of-hours pathway or the emergency department.
This page does not diagnose symptoms or decide whether it is safe to stay at home. You do not need to know which medicine caused a symptom before calling.
Treat urothelial cancer before surgery, after surgery, or in advanced disease according to the prescribed indication.

Methotrexate interferes with folate-dependent reactions that cells need to make DNA. This can slow cancer-cell division, while also affecting blood-cell production and the lining of the mouth and bowel.

What to watch forTell the pharmacist about all painkillers, antibiotics, supplements and other medicines because interactions can increase methotrexate toxicity. Report new cough or breathlessness, mouth ulcers, unusual bleeding, jaundice, reduced urine or severe rash promptly.
Vinblastine prevents cells from separating normally when they divide. It can also affect blood cells, nerves and bowel movement.
What to watch forReport constipation, abdominal swelling, numbness or pain around the drip.
Doxorubicin interacts with DNA and topoisomerase II, disrupting copying and repair. Its heart and tissue effects require particular care.

What to watch forFollow the unit’s cisplatin hydration plan and individual fluid target. The source advises 2–3 litres on Day 1 to reduce bladder irritation from cyclophosphamide; the team must adapt this if heart or kidney problems restrict fluids. Report blood in urine or painful urination promptly.

Cisplatin forms links in DNA that interfere with copying and repair. This helps stop cancer cells dividing, but healthy tissues may also be affected. Kidney protection with fluids and monitoring is central to cisplatin treatment.
What to watch forReport ringing in the ears, hearing changes, numbness or loss of function. Tell the team if you cannot drink, are passing less urine or become swollen or breathless during fluids.
The drawings are simplified explanations of drug action, not anatomical pictures or a prediction of response.
This shows treatment timing, not guaranteed symptom-free days. Your team confirms the active phase and dates.

Methotrexate is given on days 1, 15 and 22; vinblastine on days 2, 15 and 22; doxorubicin and cisplatin on day 2. The cycle repeats every 28 days. NCCP specifies three cycles before surgery, four after surgery, or up to six in metastatic disease; your team records which applies.

This is conventional 28-day MVAC, not the 14-day granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (white-cell growth support) (G-CSF)-supported schedule. Do not copy its cycle count, G-CSF timing or day-15/day-22 appointments into another regimen.
Safety testing and cancer-response assessment have different purposes. Your plan may change after illness or a dose adjustment.
Check infection-fighting cells, haemoglobin and platelets.
Check safe drug handling and detect organ effects.
Assess cancer control separately from safety blood tests.
Detect cisplatin electrolyte, hearing and nerve effects.
Urothelial cancer · treatment intent must be specified
Safety tests and symptomsNCCP

Full blood count, kidney and liver tests, ECG, review of hearing, nerves, bowel function, medicines and any fluid collections. Hearing testing is arranged when indicated. Doxorubicin schedules need cardiac assessment and echocardiogram/MUGA if over 65 or clinically indicated, with lifetime anthracycline exposure reviewed.

Full blood count, kidney and liver tests before each cycle; blood count and kidney tests before days 15 and 22. Review infection, mouth, bowel, hearing, nerves, cardiac symptoms and cumulative doxorubicin exposure.
Extra tests may be needed for symptoms, infection or abnormal results.
Follow abnormal results and ongoing symptoms until a plan is agreed.
Medicines and practical careNCCP
Confirm each treatment day, blood-test appointments, support medicines and any growth-factor or folinic-acid prescription.

Treatment is given intravenously. Methotrexate and vinblastine are short administrations; where used, doxorubicin is given through carefully checked access. Cisplatin requires prescribed hydration and a longer visit. The team confirms exact administration and observation times.

Use one written anti-sickness plan, including medicines before treatment, tablets for home and rescue treatment. Your team reconciles steroids, interactions and any stomach-protection medicine from your local prescription. Cisplatin needs prescribed intravenous fluids and electrolyte monitoring/replacement. Follow your own fluid advice; tell the team about heart failure or fluid restriction. Review kidney function, hearing, nerves and other medicines before treatment. Methotrexate interacts with several medicines, including some antibiotics, anti-inflammatory painkillers and proton-pump inhibitors. Do not start, stop or combine medicines without oncology/pharmacy advice. The aprepitant–vinblastine interaction also requires pharmacy reconciliation.

Your team reconciles steroids, interactions and any stomach-protection medicine from your local prescription. Cisplatin needs prescribed intravenous fluids and electrolyte monitoring/replacement. SWOG 8710 compared three cycles of MVAC followed by bladder-removal surgery with surgery alone. Median overall survival was 77 versus 46 months; the two-sided survival comparison had P=0.06. No residual cancer at surgery was found in 38% versus 15%.

The survival comparison did not meet the conventional two-sided 0.05 threshold. These results concern neoadjuvant treatment followed by surgery and must not be presented as an adjuvant or metastatic benefit estimate.

Timing and directions

Continuous during chemotherapyRinse 1 mL around the mouth four times daily after meals during the chemotherapy regimen.

4 mg STAT, then 2 mg PO QDS PRN
Chemotherapy-induced diarrhoea; max 16 mg/dayTake 4 mg after the first episode of diarrhoea, then 2 mg after each further episode, to a maximum of 16 mg/day.

unique_source_inventory.text: Severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain: call emergency services. Do not wait for an online answer.

Temperature 37.5°C or higher, 36°C or lower, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell — even with a normal temperature. Call oncology immediately for fever, shaking chills, suddenly feeling unwell, unusual bleeding, new breathlessness, very little urine, severe rash or vomiting that prevents drinking. Follow your hospital’s temperature and contact instructions. Severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, collapse or seizures: call 112/999.

Follow the urgent contact instructions from your treating hospital. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Outside clinic hours, use your instructed out-of-hours pathway or the emergency department.
This page does not diagnose symptoms or decide whether it is safe to stay at home. You do not need to know which medicine caused a symptom before calling.
Support radiotherapy in treating bladder cancer while aiming to preserve the bladder in selected patients.
Mitomycin damages the DNA that dividing cells need. With fluorouracil it helps radiotherapy act against bladder cancer. Healthy marrow and other tissues can also be affected.
What to watch forReport fever, unusual bruising, reduced urine, breathlessness or pain around the drip promptly.

Fluorouracil, often shortened to 5-FU, interferes with the building blocks used to make DNA and RNA, which cells need to grow. It runs through a vein over the prescribed hours. Dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (DPD) is an enzyme that breaks it down. Testing for DPD deficiency before treatment reduces risk but cannot rule out every severe reaction.
What to watch forReport severe diarrhoea, mouth sores, chest pain, sudden confusion, sore palms or soles, or unexpectedly early severe symptoms.
The drawings are simplified explanations of drug action, not anatomical pictures or a prediction of response.
This shows treatment timing, not guaranteed symptom-free days. Your team confirms the active phase and dates.

Mitomycin is given once on day 1. Fluorouracil runs continuously through a pump over 120 hours on days 1–5 and again on days 22–26, alongside the prescribed radiotherapy course. This is one chemoradiation course, not a repeating 28-day chemotherapy cycle.
NCCP 00450 is the bladder chemoradiation schedule with five-day fluorouracil infusions. Radiotherapy fractions and appointments are prescribed separately; the timeline is an educational reference.
Mitomycin and two fluorouracil pump periods support the same radiotherapy course.
The three columns show sequence, not equal durations. Fluorouracil accompanies radiation fractions 1–5 and 16–20; radiation dose and appointments are prescribed separately.
After treatment: continue symptom support and attend planned bladder surveillance. Surgery may be needed for persistent or returning cancer.
Educational reference, not a personal appointment calendar. NCCP 00450 v5, page 1

Check safe drug handling and detect organ effects.

Full blood count, kidney and liver tests weekly. Review mouth, bowel, skin, urinary and cardiac symptoms and the pump/line. Additional tests depend on symptoms or abnormal results.
Extra tests may be needed for symptoms, infection or abnormal results.
Follow abnormal results and ongoing symptoms until a plan is agreed.
Medicines and practical careNCCP
Confirm the DPD result, pump training, connection/disconnection appointments and the radiotherapy department’s bladder-preparation instructions.

Mitomycin is given through a carefully checked intravenous line. Each fluorouracil pump provides 500 mg/m² per day for five days, a total of 2500 mg/m² over 120 hours. The unit arranges pump connection, disconnection and line care.

Use one written anti-sickness plan, including medicines before treatment, tablets for home and rescue treatment. Your team reconciles steroids, interactions and any stomach-protection medicine from your local prescription. Ask for a written mouth-care and diarrhoea plan, pump contacts and line-care instructions. Stomach protection and other local adjuncts should be reconciled with the actual prescription.
Review lasting effects, support needs and any line/pump removal.
Cancer treatment and follow-upNCCP

Radiotherapy treats the bladder locally while chemotherapy makes cancer cells more sensitive to it. The radiation oncology team specifies dose, fractions and preparation. Follow-up bladder examinations are essential, and surgery may still be required if treatment does not control the cancer.
Your consultant sets scan and response-review timing for your cancer and treatment intent. Safety blood tests do not by themselves show whether treatment is working.
Agree oncology/urology follow-up and the next treatment or surveillance plan.

Trained staff connect a prescribed 120-hour fluorouracil infusion on each scheduled start day.
Each pump runs for 120 hours. Carry it as shown; never change the settings yourself.
The team confirms the exact disconnection time from the actual connection time. Keep the appointment even if the pump appears empty.
Pump disconnection does not remove a port or PICC. Agree ongoing line care and any separate removal appointment.

A port is a small chamber beneath the skin, usually on the chest, attached to a tube ending in a large vein. A special needle goes through the skin into the port when it is used. A PICC enters a vein in the upper arm; a short section remains outside under a dressing. Both can deliver a home infusion. Your team helps choose the device and teaches its care.

Tell the team about allergies, blood thinners, infections and any other cancer medicines. Follow the instructions about eating, drinking and transport; do not stop medicines yourself. Port placement uses local anaesthetic, sometimes with sedation or general anaesthetic. The team explains the procedure and risks, including infection, bleeding, clots and insertion complications. Ask how to manage discomfort, protect the wound and resume activity. Report increasing pain, redness, swelling, discharge or fever.

The nurse checks the line and treatment, secures the connection and dressing, and starts the pump. Before leaving, you should have the disconnection location and time, contact numbers including out of hours, and the written spill instructions. Ask to be shown what normal pump progress looks like. You do not need to calculate a rate.

Use the supplied carrier and the position recommended for your pump. Keep tubing free from pulling and kinks. Ask how to place the pump safely for sleep and how to protect the line and dressing when washing. Do not immerse it or swim. Avoid direct heat and cold. An elastomeric pump has a balloon that shrinks slowly and may have no alarm; an electronic pump has different instructions. Follow the instructions for the device you actually receive.

Keep the appointment even if the pump looks empty, unless the team changes the plan. Staff check the pump and line and arrange safe disposal. After flushing and other line care as required, the port needle may be removed and a small dressing applied. The implanted port stays in place until a separate removal procedure is arranged. A PICC remains in place and needs scheduled dressing and flushing care.

Call the team immediately if the pump leaks, is damaged, finishes unexpectedly early, appears not to run, or the line disconnects. Follow the emergency or spill steps you have been specifically taught, including use of a clamp if instructed. Do not reconnect, change settings or disconnect the pump yourself. Keep other people away from leaked medicine. If medicine touches skin, rinse it off and wash with soap and water, then seek advice.

Contact oncology immediately for pain or swelling around the line, a wet/loose dressing, redness, fever, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell. A painful swollen arm or neck needs urgent advice. Severe chest pain, major breathing difficulty or collapse: call 112 / 999. Do not wait for pump disconnection or the next clinic visit.
Agree the arrangements with your oncology team.

A suitable central line and ambulatory pump are usually used for the continuous fluorouracil infusions. Call the unit immediately about leaking, disconnection, alarms, redness, pain or swelling; never change the infusion rate yourself.
Confirm the next treatment, tests and any scan before leaving.

Report new or worsening symptoms promptly.

Call oncology immediately for fever, shaking chills, suddenly feeling unwell, unusual bleeding, new breathlessness, very little urine, severe rash or vomiting that prevents drinking. Follow your hospital’s temperature and contact instructions. Severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, collapse or seizures: call 112/999.
Tell the nurse immediately about flushing, rash, chills, breathlessness, faintness or pain/swelling at the infusion site.
Keep verified daytime and out-of-hours oncology numbers with your treatment card. The QR website is information, not an emergency service.

In BC2001, 360 people were randomised to bladder radiotherapy with or without fluorouracil and mitomycin. Two-year freedom from locoregional disease was 67% with chemoradiation versus 54% with radiotherapy alone (hazard ratio 0.68, 95% confidence interval 0.48–0.96).

This demonstrates improved local control compared with radiotherapy alone; it does not prove superiority to bladder-removal surgery. Overall survival was not significantly different in the primary report. Suitability for bladder preservation requires multidisciplinary assessment.

Support radiotherapy in treating bladder cancer while aiming to preserve the bladder in selected patients. Radiotherapy treats the bladder locally while chemotherapy makes cancer cells more sensitive to it. The radiation oncology team specifies dose, fractions and preparation. Follow-up bladder examinations are essential, and surgery may still be required if treatment does not control the cancer.
No. Blood counts, organ function and symptoms can make a delay or dose change safer. Your team decides whether and when to give the next dose.
Use your verified oncology daytime or out-of-hours number. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Severe symptoms require 112/999.

Dose / route / frequency
Timing and directions
100,000 units/mL, 1 mL PO QDS
Continuous during chemotherapyRinse 1 mL around the mouth four times daily after meals during the chemotherapy regimen.
Chlorhexidine mouthwash
Continuous during chemotherapyRinse 10 mL around the mouth for at least 1 minute four times daily; expel after rinsing.
As required during chemotherapyTake one tablet three times daily as required.
4 mg STAT, then 2 mg PO QDS PRN
Chemotherapy-induced diarrhoea; max 16 mg/dayTake 4 mg after the first episode of diarrhoea, then 2 mg after each further episode, to a maximum of 16 mg/day.
Reconcile all prescribed adjuncts including any local stomach-protection medicine. Follow one prescription; do not duplicate steroid or antiemetic courses.
Metoclopramide: adult maximum 10 mg up to TDS (30 mg/day) and maximum treatment duration 5 days under current EMA/Irish product information; avoid prolonged repeated use without review.
Retain and reconcile local prescribed adjuncts, including stomach protection where prescribed. This template does not issue a patient prescription.

Continuous five-day fluorouracil: NCIS multi-day guidance requires an individually agreed schedule appropriate to each treatment day and two days afterwards. The single-visit reference row does not by itself prescribe the complete pump-period course.

unique_source_inventory.text: Severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain: call emergency services. Do not wait for an online answer.

Temperature 37.5°C or higher, 36°C or lower, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell — even with a normal temperature. Call oncology immediately for fever, shaking chills, suddenly feeling unwell, unusual bleeding, new breathlessness, very little urine, severe rash or vomiting that prevents drinking. Follow your hospital’s temperature and contact instructions. Severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, collapse or seizures: call 112/999.

Follow the urgent contact instructions from your treating hospital. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Outside clinic hours, use your instructed out-of-hours pathway or the emergency department.
This page does not diagnose symptoms or decide whether it is safe to stay at home. You do not need to know which medicine caused a symptom before calling.
Aim for lasting cancer control or cure in selected relapsed germ-cell cancer, using high-dose chemotherapy with your own stored stem cells.

Carboplatin is a platinum-containing chemotherapy. Inside cells, it forms chemical attachments to DNA, including links that stop DNA strands working normally. This disrupts copying and repair and can lead to cell death. Healthy cells can also be injured, especially blood-forming cells in the bone marrow. The kidneys help remove carboplatin, so kidney function is used to calculate the dose. AUC 5 describes a target drug exposure over time; it is not a fixed dose of 5 mg.

What to watch forLow blood counts, nausea and vomiting can occur. An allergic reaction is also possible: tell the nurse immediately if you feel flushed, itchy, tight-chested or unwell during the drip.
Etoposide interferes with an enzyme used to copy and repair DNA. This can stop cancer cells growing and can also lower healthy blood counts.
What to watch forReport fever, bleeding, a sore mouth or feeling faint during an infusion.
The drawings are simplified explanations of drug action, not anatomical pictures or a prediction of response.
This shows treatment timing, not guaranteed symptom-free days. Your team confirms the active phase and dates.

Carboplatin AUC7 is followed by etoposide 750 mg/m² on days −5, −4 and −3. Your stored stem cells are infused on day 0. Growth-factor injections start on day +1 and continue until the team confirms neutrophil recovery. These day numbers are relative to the stem-cell infusion.
A specialist conditioning and rescue pathway. The diagram is a relative reference, not an outpatient 28-day reference view or a discharge prediction.

Confirm admission, stored stem-cell availability, fertility discussion and the complete transplant-support prescription before conditioning.

Chemotherapy and stem-cell rescue take place in a specialist transplant service. Carboplatin runs over 30 minutes and etoposide over two hours on each treatment day. Preparation, fluid management and monitoring add time. Staff give stem-cell infusion premedication under the local plan.

Prescribed anti-sickness treatment is needed across the high-dose days. The local transplant plan includes antiviral and antifungal prevention, mouth care, a proton-pump inhibitor and Pneumocystis pneumonia prevention. Co-trimoxazole starts only after engraftment; the team specifies the stop date. Irradiated cellular blood components are required from one week before conditioning until 12 months after stem-cell infusion.
Review lasting effects, support needs and any line/pump removal.
Cancer treatment and follow-upNCCP

Your stem cells help restore blood-cell production after intensive chemotherapy; they are not donor cells. A second high-dose course may be considered after recovery, at least 28 days later, depending on response and toxicity. Later oral etoposide is only considered in selected responders after two courses and is not automatic.
Your consultant sets scan and response-review timing for your cancer and treatment intent. Safety blood tests do not by themselves show whether treatment is working.

There are no guaranteed “safe days”. Follow your own prescription and hospital instructions. This information supports a discussion; it does not authorise treatment.

Carboplatin AUC7 is followed by etoposide 750 mg/m² on days −5, −4 and −3. Your stored stem cells are infused on day 0. Growth-factor injections start on day +1 and continue until the team confirms neutrophil recovery. These day numbers are relative to the stem-cell infusion. Follow the transplant-team plan.
Continue prescribed support and daily tests. This is not a period free of treatment risks. Report symptoms to the transplant team.
The transplant service gives the infusion and monitors you. Tell staff immediately about any reaction.
Growth factor starts on day+1. Recovery may extend beyond this illustrated interval. Daily monitoring and infection precautions continue until the team changes the plan.
Agree the arrangements with your oncology team.
The transplant team arranges suitable intravenous access and line care. Record that you require irradiated cellular blood components and tell every treating service.
Confirm the next treatment, tests and any scan before leaving.

Confirm admission, stored stem-cell availability, fertility discussion and the complete transplant-support prescription before conditioning. Prescribed anti-sickness treatment is needed across the high-dose days. The local transplant plan includes antiviral and antifungal prevention, mouth care, a proton-pump inhibitor and Pneumocystis pneumonia prevention. Co-trimoxazole starts only after engraftment; the team specifies the stop date. Irradiated cellular blood components are required from one week before conditioning until 12 months after stem-cell infusion.
Discuss fertility preservation before treatment, effective contraception, pregnancy prevention and breastfeeding. Your team must specify the precautions and duration for every medicine in your plan.
Checks help the team decide whether treatment is safe.
Follow the written plan agreed with your team.
Report new or worsening symptoms promptly.

Call oncology immediately for fever, shaking chills, suddenly feeling unwell, unusual bleeding, new breathlessness, very little urine, severe rash or vomiting that prevents drinking. Follow your hospital’s temperature and contact instructions. Severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, collapse or seizures: call 112/999.
Tell the nurse immediately about flushing, rash, chills, breathlessness, faintness or pain/swelling at the infusion site.
Keep verified daytime and out-of-hours oncology numbers with your treatment card. The QR website is information, not an emergency service.

In a retrospective series of 184 previously treated patients, 116 remained in complete remission without relapse during a median follow-up of 48 months. Three treatment-related deaths and three later cases of acute leukaemia were reported.

This was not a randomised comparison. It used carboplatin 700 mg/m², whereas NCCP 00453 uses AUC7. The study supports the treatment approach but its dose and outcomes must not be presented as identical to this protocol.

Aim for lasting cancer control or cure in selected relapsed germ-cell cancer, using high-dose chemotherapy with your own stored stem cells. Your stem cells help restore blood-cell production after intensive chemotherapy; they are not donor cells. A second high-dose course may be considered after recovery, at least 28 days later, depending on response and toxicity. Later oral etoposide is only considered in selected responders after two courses and is not automatic.
No. Blood counts, organ function and symptoms can make a delay or dose change safer. Your team decides whether and when to give the next dose.
Use your verified oncology daytime or out-of-hours number. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Severe symptoms require 112/999.

unique_source_inventory.text: Severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain: call emergency services. Do not wait for an online answer.

Temperature 37.5°C or higher, 36°C or lower, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell — even with a normal temperature. Call oncology immediately for fever, shaking chills, suddenly feeling unwell, unusual bleeding, new breathlessness, very little urine, severe rash or vomiting that prevents drinking. Follow your hospital’s temperature and contact instructions. Severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, collapse or seizures: call 112/999.

Follow the urgent contact instructions from your treating hospital. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Outside clinic hours, use your instructed out-of-hours pathway or the emergency department.
This page does not diagnose symptoms or decide whether it is safe to stay at home. You do not need to know which medicine caused a symptom before calling.
Help control advanced kidney cancer using immunotherapy and a blood-vessel-growth inhibitor.
Pembrolizumab blocks PD-1, a signal that can limit the activity of immune cells. This can help them attack cancer, but can also cause inflammation in healthy organs during treatment or after it ends.
What to watch forReport new diarrhoea, cough, breathlessness, rash, headache, unusual weakness, thirst or changes in urine promptly.

Axitinib blocks vascular endothelial growth factor receptors (VEGFRs), signals that help tumours grow new blood vessels. Reducing this blood supply can slow cancer growth. The same action explains effects on blood pressure, kidneys, bleeding and wound healing.

What to watch forCollect a prescription for diarrhoea medicine, usually loperamide, before starting. Follow the supplied instructions and contact the team for persistent diarrhoea, dizziness, poor intake or reduced urine.
The drawings are simplified explanations of drug action, not anatomical pictures or a prediction of response.
This shows treatment timing, not guaranteed symptom-free days. Your team confirms the active phase and dates.

Pembrolizumab 200 mg is given intravenously every 21 days. Axitinib starts at 5 mg twice daily, about 12 hours apart, continuously, with or without food. Only your team may change the dose. Do not take an extra axitinib dose after a missed or vomited dose. Duration depends on benefit, tolerance and the agreed plan.

Pembrolizumab is held or stopped for toxicity, never dose-reduced. Axitinib has separate dose levels and holding rules. Liver injury or diarrhoea can involve either medicine, so do not attribute symptoms or change tablets without advice.
Safety testing and cancer-response assessment have different purposes. Your plan may change after illness or a dose adjustment.

unique_source_inventory.text: Severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain: call emergency services. Do not wait for an online answer.

Temperature 37.5°C or higher, 36°C or lower, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell — even with a normal temperature. Call oncology immediately for fever, shaking chills, suddenly feeling unwell, unusual bleeding, new breathlessness, very little urine, severe rash or vomiting that prevents drinking. Follow your hospital’s temperature and contact instructions. Severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, collapse or seizures: call 112/999.

Follow the urgent contact instructions from your treating hospital. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Outside clinic hours, use your instructed out-of-hours pathway or the emergency department.
This page does not diagnose symptoms or decide whether it is safe to stay at home. You do not need to know which medicine caused a symptom before calling.
Treat relapsed or resistant testicular germ-cell cancer, with the possibility of lasting remission in selected patients.

Cells use tiny structures called microtubules to separate their chromosomes when dividing. Paclitaxel stabilises these structures so they cannot rearrange normally, interrupting cell division. It can also affect nerves and other healthy tissues.

What to watch forReport tingling or numbness before the next dose, especially if it affects walking or hand use. Tell the nurse immediately about flushing, chest or throat tightness, itching, dizziness or breathing changes during infusion.
Ifosfamide damages cancer-cell DNA. Its breakdown products can also affect the bladder, kidneys and brain. Mesna protects the bladder but does not prevent all kidney or brain effects.
What to watch forReport confusion, sleepiness, blood in urine or reduced urine immediately.

Cisplatin forms links in DNA that interfere with copying and repair. This helps stop cancer cells dividing, but healthy tissues may also be affected. Kidney protection with fluids and monitoring is central to cisplatin treatment.
What to watch forReport ringing in the ears, hearing changes, numbness or loss of function. Tell the team if you cannot drink, are passing less urine or become swollen or breathless during fluids.

Paclitaxel is given on day 1. Cisplatin and ifosfamide are given on days 1–5, with bladder-protecting mesna each day. Growth-factor injections start on day 6 until neutrophil recovery under local policy. Four 21-day cycles are planned, subject to consultant review.
This is NCCP 00602: paclitaxel175 mg/m² day 1, ifosfamide1200 mg/m² and cisplatin20 mg/m² days 1–5. Other published TIP schedules differ.
Safety testing and cancer-response assessment have different purposes. Your plan may change after illness or a dose adjustment.

Paclitaxel runs over three hours on day 1, cisplatin over one hour and ifosfamide over two hours on days 1–5. Mesna is given immediately before ifosfamide and again four and eight hours after the ifosfamide infusion finishes. The unit coordinates the complete schedule; do not calculate home timings yourself.

Cisplatin needs a high-risk anti-sickness plan and prescribed hydration/electrolytes. Ifosfamide needs mesna and adequate fluids. Paclitaxel needs prescribed allergy premedication; reconcile steroid doses with antiemetics. Aprepitant may increase ifosfamide brain toxicity, so pharmacy must review the combination. Growth factor is included from day 6. Retain prescribed mouth care, pain relief and stomach protection.

required_units.text: Space for your own cycle or review record, questions and notes, followed by your treatment card.
Gemcitabine + split-dose cisplatinNational Cancer Control Programme (NCCP) 00622

Record each cycle separately. Each medicine has its own symptom table. Mark the worst symptoms since your last review, when they occurred and what they stopped you doing. Overlapping symptoms can be recorded under more than one medicine; you do not have to identify the cause.

These are patient-language severity prompts, not a validated questionnaire or a formal Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) grading tool. Your team assigns the clinical grade. Serious symptoms override the columns: call without waiting to decide a severity level.
Use a new record sheet for each cycle or review. Copy or print another sheet when needed; the number of sheets does not prescribe the length of treatment.
Source-reconciled feasibility draft; independent clinician, pharmacy and patient review pending.
Bring this record to every treatment and review; your team confirms the dose and next appointment.
Both medicines on days 1 and 8 · every 21 days · copy this sheet for another cycle of the same phase.

unique_source_inventory.text: Severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain: call emergency services. Do not wait for an online answer.

Temperature 37.5°C or higher, 36°C or lower, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell — even with a normal temperature. Call oncology immediately for fever, shaking chills, suddenly feeling unwell, unusual bleeding, new breathlessness, very little urine, severe rash or vomiting that prevents drinking. Follow your hospital’s temperature and contact instructions. Severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, collapse or seizures: call 112/999.

Follow the urgent contact instructions from your treating hospital. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Outside clinic hours, use your instructed out-of-hours pathway or the emergency department.
This page does not diagnose symptoms or decide whether it is safe to stay at home. You do not need to know which medicine caused a symptom before calling.
Help control advanced urothelial cancer and its symptoms.
Gemcitabine interferes with making DNA, which dividing cancer cells need. Healthy blood-forming cells and other tissues can also be affected.
What to watch forReport fever, unusual bleeding, breathlessness, rash, swelling or reduced urine promptly.

Cisplatin forms links in DNA that interfere with copying and repair. This helps stop cancer cells dividing, but healthy tissues may also be affected. Kidney protection with fluids and monitoring is central to cisplatin treatment.
What to watch forReport ringing in the ears, hearing changes, numbness or loss of function. Tell the team if you cannot drink, are passing less urine or become swollen or breathless during fluids.
The drawings are simplified explanations of drug action, not anatomical pictures or a prediction of response.
This shows treatment timing, not guaranteed symptom-free days. Your team confirms the active phase and dates.
Gemcitabine and cisplatin are both given on days 1 and 8 of a 21-day cycle, usually for four to six cycles. Cisplatin is split into two 35 mg/m² doses; do not use another GemCis calendar.

NCCP 00622 uses cisplatin 35 mg/m² on both days 1 and 8. Its impaired-renal-function indication and creatinine clearance (CrCl) <60 exclusion need clinical reconciliation; a split dose does not itself prove cisplatin is safe.
Safety testing and cancer-response assessment have different purposes. Your plan may change after illness or a dose adjustment.

The local CUH source is retained as a reference list, not as the national antiemetic standard. Nystatin/chlorhexidine are displayed as local mouth-care adjuncts, not universal antiemetic or mucositis prophylaxis. Verify current local oral-care policy. This historical supplied proforma requires current local pharmacy confirmation. It is an alternative/local reference, not an additional set of medicines to combine automatically with the national plan.
Dose / route / frequency
Timing and directions
Day 1Take one capsule one hour prior to chemotherapy; bring it to the day ward.
Days 2-3Take one capsule daily for two days starting the day after chemotherapy.
Days 2-4Take once daily for three days starting the day after chemotherapy.
Days 1-4Take one capsule daily for four days starting on the day of chemotherapy.
100,000 units/mL, 1 mL PO QDS
Continuous during chemotherapyRinse 1 mL around the mouth four times daily after meals during the chemotherapy regimen.
Chlorhexidine mouthwash
Continuous during chemotherapyRinse 10 mL around the mouth for at least 1 minute four times daily; expel after rinsing.
As required during chemotherapyTake one tablet three times daily as required.
4 mg STAT, then 2 mg PO QDS PRN
Chemotherapy-induced diarrhoea; max 16 mg/dayTake 4 mg after the first episode of diarrhoea, then 2 mg after each further episode, to a maximum of 16 mg/day.
Reconcile all prescribed adjuncts including any local stomach-protection medicine. Follow one prescription; do not duplicate steroid or antiemetic courses.
Caution: metoclopramide with olanzapine may increase extrapyramidal adverse effects.
Dexamethasone may be modified or omitted where the systemic anticancer therapy (SACT) regimen already includes a steroid.
Metoclopramide: adult maximum 10 mg up to TDS (30 mg/day) and maximum treatment duration 5 days under current EMA/Irish product information; avoid prolonged repeated use without review.
Retain and reconcile local prescribed adjuncts, including stomach protection where prescribed. This template does not issue a patient prescription.

Before signing: verify allergies, current medicines, interactions, renal / hepatic function, QT risk, sedation, prior response, total steroid exposure and the rescue-medicine duration. Do not duplicate medicines from another phase.

unique_source_inventory.text: Severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain: call emergency services. Do not wait for an online answer.

Temperature 37.5°C or higher, 36°C or lower, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell — even with a normal temperature. Call oncology immediately for fever, shaking chills, suddenly feeling unwell, unusual bleeding, new breathlessness, very little urine, severe rash or vomiting that prevents drinking. Follow your hospital’s temperature and contact instructions. Severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, collapse or seizures: call 112/999.

Follow the urgent contact instructions from your treating hospital. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Outside clinic hours, use your instructed out-of-hours pathway or the emergency department.
This page does not diagnose symptoms or decide whether it is safe to stay at home. You do not need to know which medicine caused a symptom before calling.
Reduce the risk of upper-tract urothelial cancer returning after surgery.
Gemcitabine interferes with making DNA, which dividing cancer cells need. Healthy blood-forming cells and other tissues can also be affected.
What to watch forReport fever, unusual bleeding, breathlessness, rash, swelling or reduced urine promptly.

Cisplatin forms links in DNA that interfere with copying and repair. This helps stop cancer cells dividing, but healthy tissues may also be affected. Kidney protection with fluids and monitoring is central to cisplatin treatment.
What to watch forReport ringing in the ears, hearing changes, numbness or loss of function. Tell the team if you cannot drink, are passing less urine or become swollen or breathless during fluids.
The drawings are simplified explanations of drug action, not anatomical pictures or a prediction of response.
This shows treatment timing, not guaranteed symptom-free days. Your team confirms the active phase and dates.

Gemcitabine is given on days 1 and 8 and cisplatin on day 1. The 21-day cycle is planned four times after surgery for eligible upper-tract urothelial cancer. Treatment may be delayed or adjusted for safety.

NCCP 00628 is an adjuvant upper-tract regimen for muscle-invasive and/or node-positive, non-metastatic predominantly transitional-cell disease. It is not the advanced-disease 28-day or split-dose GemCis regimen.
Safety testing and cancer-response assessment have different purposes. Your plan may change after illness or a dose adjustment.

POUT randomised 261 people after surgery for high-risk upper-tract urothelial cancer to four cycles of gemcitabine/platinum or surveillance. At five years, disease-free survival was 62% versus 45% (hazard ratio 0.55, 95% confidence interval 0.38–0.80).

Disease-free survival means being alive without a recorded recurrence; it is not the same as overall survival. The trial included cisplatin or carboplatin according to kidney function, so the whole-trial result is not a cisplatin-only estimate or permission for automatic substitution.

No. Blood counts, organ function and symptoms can make a delay or dose change safer. Your team decides whether and when to give the next dose.

Dose / route / frequency
Timing and directions
Day 1Take one capsule one hour prior to chemotherapy; bring it to the day ward.
Days 2-3Take one capsule daily for two days starting the day after chemotherapy.
Days 2-4Take once daily for three days starting the day after chemotherapy.
Days 1-4Take one capsule daily for four days starting on the day of chemotherapy.
100,000 units/mL, 1 mL PO QDS
Continuous during chemotherapyRinse 1 mL around the mouth four times daily after meals during the chemotherapy regimen.
Chlorhexidine mouthwash
Continuous during chemotherapyRinse 10 mL around the mouth for at least 1 minute four times daily; expel after rinsing.
As required during chemotherapyTake one tablet three times daily as required.
4 mg STAT, then 2 mg PO QDS PRN
Chemotherapy-induced diarrhoea; max 16 mg/dayTake 4 mg after the first episode of diarrhoea, then 2 mg after each further episode, to a maximum of 16 mg/day.
Reconcile all prescribed adjuncts including any local stomach-protection medicine. Follow one prescription; do not duplicate steroid or antiemetic courses.
Caution: metoclopramide with olanzapine may increase extrapyramidal adverse effects.
Dexamethasone may be modified or omitted where the systemic anticancer therapy (SACT) regimen already includes a steroid.
Metoclopramide: adult maximum 10 mg up to TDS (30 mg/day) and maximum treatment duration 5 days under current EMA/Irish product information; avoid prolonged repeated use without review.

unique_source_inventory.text: Severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain: call emergency services. Do not wait for an online answer.

Temperature 37.5°C or higher, 36°C or lower, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell — even with a normal temperature. Call oncology immediately for fever, shaking chills, suddenly feeling unwell, unusual bleeding, new breathlessness, very little urine, severe rash or vomiting that prevents drinking. Follow your hospital’s temperature and contact instructions. Severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, collapse or seizures: call 112/999.

Follow the urgent contact instructions from your treating hospital. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Outside clinic hours, use your instructed out-of-hours pathway or the emergency department.
This page does not diagnose symptoms or decide whether it is safe to stay at home. You do not need to know which medicine caused a symptom before calling.
Help radiotherapy treat bladder cancer as part of a selected bladder-preservation plan.
Gemcitabine interferes with making DNA, which dividing cancer cells need. Healthy blood-forming cells and other tissues can also be affected.
What to watch forReport fever, unusual bleeding, breathlessness, rash, swelling or reduced urine promptly.
The drawings are simplified explanations of drug action, not anatomical pictures or a prediction of response.
This shows treatment timing, not guaranteed symptom-free days. Your team confirms the active phase and dates.

Gemcitabine 100 mg/m² is given weekly on days 1, 8, 15 and 22, two to four hours before radiotherapy. There are four planned gemcitabine doses in one course. This low-dose schedule is different from gemcitabine 1000 mg/m² chemotherapy.
NCCP 00759 is four weekly 100 mg/m² gemcitabine doses with radiotherapy. Do not import a 1000 mg/m² gemcitabine dose, repeated chemotherapy cycles or another radiotherapy prescription.
The chemotherapy and radiotherapy teams coordinate the appointments.
One four-dose course. The graphic does not prescribe radiation dose, fractions or extra gemcitabine cycles.
After treatment: continue the symptom plan and attend bladder and cancer follow-up.

Your consultant sets scan and response-review timing for your cancer and treatment intent. Safety blood tests do not by themselves show whether treatment is working.

Call oncology immediately for fever, shaking chills, suddenly feeling unwell, unusual bleeding, new breathlessness, very little urine, severe rash or vomiting that prevents drinking. Follow your hospital’s temperature and contact instructions. Severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, collapse or seizures: call 112/999.
Tell the nurse immediately about flushing, rash, chills, breathlessness, faintness or pain/swelling at the infusion site.
Keep verified daytime and out-of-hours oncology numbers with your treatment card. The QR website is information, not an emergency service.
GemX was a single-arm phase II study of 50 people with muscle-invasive bladder cancer. Forty-four patients, 88% of the study group, had a complete response at the bladder examination after treatment.

A complete endoscopic response is not proof of cure. This small study had no randomised comparison with surgery or other chemoradiation, so its result cannot establish which option is best for an individual.

Help radiotherapy treat bladder cancer as part of a selected bladder-preservation plan. Radiotherapy is the local cancer treatment; gemcitabine helps sensitise cancer cells to it. Radiation dose, fractions and any interruptions are agreed by radiation oncology. Regular bladder surveillance is still needed; surgery may be considered for persistent or returning cancer.
No. Blood counts, organ function and symptoms can make a delay or dose change safer. Your team decides whether and when to give the next dose.
Use your verified oncology daytime or out-of-hours number. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Severe symptoms require 112/999.

CUH Department of Medical Oncology: Adjuvant medication prescription for chemotherapy Low Risk for nausea and vomiting, Version 2 (05/05/2021)

The local CUH source is retained as a reference list, not as the national antiemetic standard. Nystatin/chlorhexidine are displayed as local mouth-care adjuncts, not universal antiemetic or mucositis prophylaxis. Verify current local oral-care policy. This historical supplied proforma requires current local pharmacy confirmation. It is an alternative/local reference, not an additional set of medicines to combine automatically with the national plan.
Dose / route / frequency
Timing and directions
100,000 units/mL, 1 mL PO QDS
Continuous during chemotherapyRinse 1 mL around the mouth four times daily after meals during the chemotherapy regimen.
Chlorhexidine mouthwash
Continuous during chemotherapyRinse 10 mL around the mouth for at least 1 minute four times daily; expel after rinsing.
As required during chemotherapyTake one tablet three times daily as required.
4 mg STAT, then 2 mg PO QDS PRN
Chemotherapy-induced diarrhoea; max 16 mg/dayTake 4 mg after the first episode of diarrhoea, then 2 mg after each further episode, to a maximum of 16 mg/day.
Reconcile all prescribed adjuncts including any local stomach-protection medicine. Follow one prescription; do not duplicate steroid or antiemetic courses.
Metoclopramide: adult maximum 10 mg up to TDS (30 mg/day) and maximum treatment duration 5 days under current EMA/Irish product information; avoid prolonged repeated use without review.
Retain and reconcile local prescribed adjuncts, including stomach protection where prescribed. This template does not issue a patient prescription.

unique_source_inventory.text: Severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain: call emergency services. Do not wait for an online answer.

Temperature 37.5°C or higher, 36°C or lower, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell — even with a normal temperature. Contact your urology or oncology treatment team immediately for fever, chills, sudden illness, severe bladder pain, persistent bleeding or inability to pass urine. Severe breathing difficulty, collapse or chest pain: call112/999.

Follow the urgent contact instructions from your treating hospital. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Outside clinic hours, use your instructed out-of-hours pathway or the emergency department.
This page does not diagnose symptoms or decide whether it is safe to stay at home. You do not need to know which medicine caused a symptom before calling.
Reduce the risk of bladder cancer returning or worsening, and treat suitable carcinoma in situ, using local immune treatment.
BCG contains weakened live bacteria. Placing it inside the bladder stimulates a local immune response against abnormal cells. It is not a checkpoint-inhibitor medicine.
What to watch forCall urgently for fever, shaking chills, marked illness, breathlessness or inability to pass urine. Always tell other clinicians about prior BCG.
The drawings are simplified explanations of drug action, not anatomical pictures or a prediction of response.
This shows treatment timing, not guaranteed symptom-free days. Your team confirms the active phase and dates.

BCG is placed in the bladder once weekly for six weeks. Maintenance uses three weekly instillations at months 3,6 and12 for intermediate-risk disease; high/very-high-risk plans may add months 18,24,30 and36. Your urologist confirms the course according to risk, response, tolerance and supply.
Live BCG placed inside the bladder. It is not intravenous chemotherapy or PD1/PDL1 checkpoint immunotherapy.
Safety testing and cancer-response assessment have different purposes. Your plan may change after illness or a dose adjustment.
Confirm diagnosis, suitability and the required safety checks.
Detect toxicity and assess response with the appropriate tests.
Non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer
Bladder checks and symptomsNCCP
Cystoscopy with biopsy or resection confirms diagnosis. The urologist reviews risk group, healing after procedures, infection, bleeding, immune suppression, medicines and the chosen BCG product.

Check symptoms and suitability before each instillation. Cystoscopy with possible biopsy and urine cytology are planned eight weeks after the last BCG dose and regularly afterwards under the urologist’s plan.
Extra tests may be needed for symptoms, infection or abnormal results.
Follow abnormal results and ongoing symptoms until a plan is agreed.
Medicines and practical careNCCP
Tell the unit about fever, urinary infection, visible blood, recent bladder surgery/biopsy, antibiotics or immune-suppressing medicines before attending.

A urinary catheter is used to place one prescribed vial of BCG into the bladder, usually in up to50 mL saline. NCCP gives a dwell time of one to two hours; BCG-medac instructions specify two hours. Staff confirm your product and how and when to empty your bladder.

Routine anti-sickness or steroid premedication is not usually needed. The source asks for no fluids for four hours before and until two hours after instillation; confirm this is safe with your team, especially with fluid-sensitive conditions. Obtain written instructions for restarting fluids, passing urine, toilet hygiene, spill management and sexual precautions for your exact product.
Review lasting effects, support needs and any line/pump removal.
Cancer treatment and follow-upNCCP

Cystoscopy surveillance remains essential after BCG. Persistent high-grade disease or progression needs a fresh specialist discussion, which may include bladder removal or other treatment. Maintenance is not proof that the cancer has been cured.
Your consultant sets scan and response-review timing for your cancer and treatment intent. Safety blood tests do not by themselves show whether treatment is working.
Agree oncology/urology follow-up and the next treatment or surveillance plan.

There are no guaranteed “safe days”. Follow your own prescription and hospital instructions. This information supports a discussion; it does not authorise treatment.
Weekly induction appointment after safety checks. Follow your confirmed appointment and support plan.

Follow the prescribed urine, symptom and contact plan. Report fever, severe pain, bleeding or difficulty passing urine promptly. The next visit depends on safety review. Follow your confirmed appointment and support plan.
Agree the arrangements with your oncology team.

Treatment uses a temporary urinary catheter, not an intravenous chemotherapy pump. Catheter trauma or bleeding may mean postponement. Do not stop prescribed medicines or diuretics without the team’s instructions.
Confirm the next treatment, tests and any scan before leaving.

Tell the unit about fever, urinary infection, visible blood, recent bladder surgery/biopsy, antibiotics or immune-suppressing medicines before attending. Routine anti-sickness or steroid premedication is not usually needed. The source asks for no fluids for four hours before and until two hours after instillation; confirm this is safe with your team, especially with fluid-sensitive conditions. Obtain written instructions for restarting fluids, passing urine, toilet hygiene, spill management and sexual precautions for your exact product.
Discuss pregnancy prevention, breastfeeding, fertility concerns and product-specific sexual precautions. Your urology team confirms the written plan.

For BCG-medac, sit to pass urine after the agreed dwell time and wash hands and genital skin carefully. Follow the unit’s written toilet-disinfection instructions. Use a condom for one week after each treatment. Carry the product alert card; tell clinicians about BCG even years later if unexplained fever or illness occurs.
Checks help the team decide whether treatment is safe.
Follow the written plan agreed with your team.
Report new or worsening symptoms promptly.

Call your treatment team immediately for fever, shaking chills, suddenly feeling unwell, unusual bleeding, new breathlessness, very little urine, severe rash or vomiting that prevents drinking. Follow your hospital’s temperature and contact instructions. Severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, collapse or seizures: call 112/999.
Tell the nurse immediately about severe pain, bleeding, catheter difficulty or an allergic reaction. The team may postpone instillation.
Keep verified daytime and out-of-hours oncology numbers with your treatment card. The QR website is information, not an emergency service.

BCG stimulates immune activity in the bladder. Maintenance can reduce recurrence and may reduce progression, but its benefit must be weighed against urinary symptoms, serious infection risk and the individual cancer risk.
The NCCP schedule allows different BCG products. Product-specific exclusions and precautions must be checked; the BCG-medac information is not permission to substitute brands without review.

Reduce the risk of bladder cancer returning or worsening, and treat suitable carcinoma in situ, using local immune treatment. Cystoscopy surveillance remains essential after BCG. Persistent high-grade disease or progression needs a fresh specialist discussion, which may include bladder removal or other treatment. Maintenance is not proof that the cancer has been cured.
No. Blood counts, organ function and symptoms can make a delay or dose change safer. Your team decides whether and when to give the next dose.
Use your verified oncology daytime or out-of-hours number. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Severe symptoms require 112/999.

required_units.text: Space for your own cycle or review record, questions and notes, followed by your treatment card.
Enfortumab vedotin · monotherapyNational Cancer Control Programme (NCCP) 00846

Record each cycle separately. Each medicine has its own symptom table. Mark the worst symptoms since your last review, when they occurred and what they stopped you doing. Overlapping symptoms can be recorded under more than one medicine; you do not have to identify the cause.

These are patient-language severity prompts, not a validated questionnaire or a formal Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) grading tool. Your team assigns the clinical grade. Serious symptoms override the columns: call without waiting to decide a severity level.
Use a new record sheet for each cycle or review. Copy or print another sheet when needed; the number of sheets does not prescribe the length of treatment.
Source-reconciled feasibility draft; independent clinician, pharmacy and patient review pending.
Bring this record to every treatment and review; your team confirms the dose and next appointment.
Days 1, 8 and 15 · every 28 days · copy this sheet for another cycle of the same phase.
□ Dry skin / hair loss: record
□ Persistent rash / skin change: contact team
□ Painful, spreading or blistering rash: urgent review
□ Severe skin reaction with acute illness: emergency help
□ New irritation: report
□ Pain, redness or light sensitivity: call promptly
□ Blurred vision / severe eye pain: urgent review
□ Sudden major vision loss: emergency assessment
□ Mild change; usual tasks unaffected
□ Limits buttons, writing or walking: call
□ Washing, dressing or walking difficult: urgent review
□ Sudden major weakness / paralysis: emergency help
□ New cough or breathlessness: call promptly
□ Symptoms with usual activity: urgent review
□ Breathless at rest: urgent assessment
□ Severe breathing difficulty / collapse: 112/999
□ New chills / feeling unwell: call
□ Fever: use the written urgent plan now
□ Fever with marked weakness: urgent assessment
□ Collapse / confusion / breathing difficulty: 112/999
□ New small bruise / brief bleed: report
□ Repeated bleeding: call today
□ Bleeding that will not stop: urgent help
□ Heavy bleeding / collapse: 112/999
□ Tiredness improves with rest
□ Rest does not help; usual tasks affected: call
□ Self-care difficult: urgent review
□ Queasy but eating and drinking
□ Intake reduced: contact the team
□ Unable to maintain intake: urgent review
□ Collapse / severe dehydration: 112/999
□ Up to 3 extra stools above normal
□ 4–6 extra stools/day or at night: call
□ 7+ extra stools/day or dehydration: urgent review
□ Collapse / severe dehydration: 112/999
Infusion-site symptoms
□ New burning or pain during infusion: tell the nurse immediately
□ Swelling, redness or leakage: tell the nurse immediately
□ Increasing pain, blistering or spreading redness: urgent review
□ Severe sudden illness or collapse: emergency help

unique_source_inventory.text: Severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain: call emergency services. Do not wait for an online answer.

Temperature 37.5°C or higher, 36°C or lower, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell — even with a normal temperature. Call oncology immediately for fever, shaking chills, suddenly feeling unwell, unusual bleeding, new breathlessness, very little urine, severe rash or vomiting that prevents drinking. Follow your hospital’s temperature and contact instructions. Severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, collapse or seizures: call 112/999.

Follow the urgent contact instructions from your treating hospital. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Outside clinic hours, use your instructed out-of-hours pathway or the emergency department.
This page does not diagnose symptoms or decide whether it is safe to stay at home. You do not need to know which medicine caused a symptom before calling.
Help control advanced urothelial cancer previously treated with platinum chemotherapy and a PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor.

An antibody attaches to a protein called nectin-4 and delivers a chemotherapy payload that disrupts cell division. Healthy skin, nerves and other tissues can also be affected. This is not a checkpoint immunotherapy medicine.
What to watch forReport any rash early, especially blistering, fever or mouth/eye/genital sores; also report thirst, frequent urination, numbness or new breathing symptoms.
The drawings are simplified explanations of drug action, not anatomical pictures or a prediction of response.
This shows treatment timing, not guaranteed symptom-free days. Your team confirms the active phase and dates.

Enfortumab vedotin is given on days 1, 8 and 15 of a 28-day cycle. The starting dose is 1.25 mg/kg, capped at 125 mg per dose. The team may hold, reduce or stop treatment for side effects. Treatment continues while appropriate according to benefit and tolerance.

Severe skin reactions may occur early, including the first cycle. High glucose, lung inflammation, neuropathy and eye problems need prompt assessment; a week without an infusion is not a guaranteed symptom-free week.
Safety testing and cancer-response assessment have different purposes. Your plan may change after illness or a dose adjustment.
Check infection-fighting cells, haemoglobin and platelets.

EV-301 randomised 608 people previously treated with platinum and a PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor. Median overall survival was 12.88 months with enfortumab versus 8.97 months with investigator-selected chemotherapy (hazard ratio 0.70, 95% confidence interval 0.56–0.89).
These group medians do not predict an individual lifespan. The result concerns later-line monotherapy and must not be substituted for evidence about first-line enfortumab/pembrolizumab.

Nystatin/chlorhexidine are displayed as local mouth-care adjuncts, not universal antiemetic or mucositis prophylaxis. Verify current local oral-care policy. This historical supplied proforma requires current local pharmacy confirmation. It is an alternative/local reference, not an additional set of medicines to combine automatically with the national plan.
Dose / route / frequency
Timing and directions
100,000 units/mL, 1 mL PO QDS
Continuous during chemotherapyRinse 1 mL around the mouth four times daily after meals during the chemotherapy regimen.
Chlorhexidine mouthwash
Continuous during chemotherapyRinse 10 mL around the mouth for at least 1 minute four times daily; expel after rinsing.
As required during chemotherapyTake one tablet three times daily as required.
4 mg STAT, then 2 mg PO QDS PRN
Chemotherapy-induced diarrhoea; max 16 mg/dayTake 4 mg after the first episode of diarrhoea, then 2 mg after each further episode, to a maximum of 16 mg/day.
Reconcile all prescribed adjuncts including any local stomach-protection medicine. Follow one prescription; do not duplicate steroid or antiemetic courses.
Metoclopramide: adult maximum 10 mg up to TDS (30 mg/day) and maximum treatment duration 5 days under current EMA/Irish product information; avoid prolonged repeated use without review.
Retain and reconcile local prescribed adjuncts, including stomach protection where prescribed. This template does not issue a patient prescription.
