unique_source_inventory.text: Severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain: call emergency services. Do not wait for an online answer.

Temperature 37.5°C or higher, 36°C or lower, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell — even with a normal temperature. Call oncology immediately for fever, shaking chills, suddenly feeling unwell, unusual bleeding, new breathlessness, very little urine, severe rash or vomiting that prevents drinking. Follow your hospital’s temperature and contact instructions. Severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, collapse or seizures: call 112/999.

Follow the urgent contact instructions from your treating hospital. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Outside clinic hours, use your instructed out-of-hours pathway or the emergency department.
This page does not diagnose symptoms or decide whether it is safe to stay at home. You do not need to know which medicine caused a symptom before calling.
Help control advanced urothelial cancer with a susceptible FGFR3 alteration after previous PD1/PDL1 treatment.

Some urothelial cancers use an altered fibroblast growth factor receptor, FGFR3, to drive growth. Erdafitinib blocks this signal. FGFR also helps regulate phosphate handling, explaining why blood phosphate may rise.
What to watch forReport any new blurred vision, visual distortion or eye pain promptly; do not wait for the next routine eye appointment.
The drawings are simplified explanations of drug action, not anatomical pictures or a prediction of response.
This shows treatment timing, not guaranteed symptom-free days. Your team confirms the active phase and dates.

The usual starting dose is8 mg once daily. The team may increase it to9 mg after reviewing phosphate and toxicity on days 14–21. Never change the dose yourself. Treatment is continuous until progression or unacceptable toxicity; the28-day view is only a reference.
The molecular result must be a susceptible FGFR3 alteration. A general FGFR result or a phosphate rise alone does not prove tumour benefit.
Safety testing and cancer-response assessment have different purposes. Your plan may change after illness or a dose adjustment.
Confirm diagnosis, suitability and the required safety checks.
Detect toxicity and assess response with the appropriate tests.
FGFR3-selected advanced urothelial cancer
Safety tests and symptomsNCCP
Confirm the FGFR3 result and previous treatment. Blood count, kidney/liver profile, phosphate, urea/electrolytes, heart history/examination, ECG and eye examination are required at baseline.

Phosphate is checked on days 14–21 and monthly afterwards, more often if elevated. Eye examinations are monthly for the first four months and every three months thereafter; new symptoms need prompt review. Repeat blood count, kidney/liver tests, electrolytes and ECG under the prescribed plan.
Extra tests may be needed for symptoms, infection or abnormal results.
Follow abnormal results and ongoing symptoms until a plan is agreed.
Medicines and practical careNCCP
Confirm the tablet strength, daily dose, early phosphate appointment and baseline eye examination before starting.

Swallow tablets whole, with or without food, at about the same time each day. Avoid grapefruit and Seville oranges. If a dose is missed, take it as soon as possible and resume the usual schedule next day; never take extra tablets. If you vomit after a dose, take the next dose the following day.

High phosphate may need a dietitian-guided phosphate restriction and prescribed phosphate binder. Do not add vitaminD supplements without oncology review. Ask about mouth care, skin/nail care, diarrhoea treatment and dry-eye support. Bring all medicines and supplements for interaction checking.
Review lasting effects, support needs and any line/pump removal.

FGFR testing selects people whose tumour may respond to this mechanism. Treatment aims to control cancer; scans and symptoms assess benefit separately from phosphate and other safety tests. Other systemic treatment or symptom-directed radiotherapy depends on your individual situation.

After previous PD1/PDL1 therapy, median overall survival was 12.1 months with erdafitinib versus 7.8 months with chemotherapy (hazard ratio0.64;95% confidence interval0.47–0.88). Median progression-free survival was 5.6 versus 2.7 months.
These are trial group estimates, not a personal prognosis. Trial molecular eligibility included FGFR3/2 alterations; the current Irish indication requires susceptible FGFR3 alterations.

unique_source_inventory.text: Severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain: call emergency services. Do not wait for an online answer.

Temperature 37.5°C or higher, 36°C or lower, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell — even with a normal temperature. Contact your urology or oncology treatment team immediately for fever, chills, sudden illness, severe bladder pain, persistent bleeding or inability to pass urine. Severe breathing difficulty, collapse or chest pain: call112/999.

Follow the urgent contact instructions from your treating hospital. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Outside clinic hours, use your instructed out-of-hours pathway or the emergency department.
This page does not diagnose symptoms or decide whether it is safe to stay at home. You do not need to know which medicine caused a symptom before calling.
Treat selected high-risk bladder cancer when BCG has not worked, cannot be tolerated or is unsuitable.
Gemcitabine is placed directly in the bladder, held there and drained before docetaxel. Local treatment limits exposure elsewhere but does not guarantee that systemic effects cannot occur.
What to watch forReport fever, persistent bleeding, severe pain or inability to pass urine.
Docetaxel is instilled after gemcitabine has been drained. It acts on dividing cells in the bladder lining. Its dose and preparation are different from intravenous docetaxel.
What to watch forDo not substitute intravenous docetaxel instructions or steroid premedication for this bladder plan.
The drawings are simplified explanations of drug action, not anatomical pictures or a prediction of response.
This shows treatment timing, not guaranteed symptom-free days. Your team confirms the active phase and dates.

Both medicines are given at each weekly induction visit for six weeks. Selected patients then receive treatment monthly for 18 months, beginning six weeks after the final induction dose. Maintenance depends on response and tolerability; it is not automatic.
Intravesical gemcitabine/docetaxel uses an unlicensed route and dose schedule in Ireland. The clinician must discuss this and follow hospital approval/consent policy.
Safety testing and cancer-response assessment have different purposes. Your plan may change after illness or a dose adjustment.
Confirm diagnosis, suitability and the required safety checks.
Detect toxicity and assess response with the appropriate tests.
High-risk non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer
Bladder checks and symptomsNCCP

Cystoscopy with biopsy or resection confirms diagnosis. Confirm healing after surgery, no recent bleeding or catheter trauma, and assess urine for infection. Tell the urologist about pregnancy, breastfeeding, allergies and bladder capacity problems.

Before treatment, urine dipstick and symptom assessment help check for infection; symptoms require urology review. Response assessment determines maintenance. If disease-free, cystoscopy with cytology is usually every three months for two years.
Extra tests may be needed for symptoms, infection or abnormal results.
Follow abnormal results and ongoing symptoms until a plan is agreed.
Medicines and practical careNCCP

Confirm the bicarbonate prescription and the fluid/diuretic plan. The source advises avoiding fluids for four hours before and until two hours after instillation, and avoiding alcohol/coffee around treatment. The team must adapt instructions for your medical conditions; do not change a prescribed diuretic yourself.

Gemcitabine1000 mg in50 mL is instilled through a urinary catheter and held for 60 minutes, then drained. Docetaxel40 mg in50 mL follows and is held for 60 minutes. The team may use90-minute dwell times. These are fixed bladder doses, not intravenous doses based on body size.

The source includes prescribed sodium bicarbonate1200 mg the night before and1200 mg one hour before treatment to reduce bladder irritation. Anti-sickness medicine may be considered if nausea followed a previous instillation. Pain or spasm medicines are individual prescriptions; ask before taking ibuprofen or other medicines.
Review lasting effects, support needs and any line/pump removal.
Cancer treatment and follow-upNCCP

This is a bladder-preserving option for selected patients. Cystoscopy remains necessary; high-grade recurrence or progression requires discussion of other options, including bladder removal where suitable.
Your consultant sets scan and response-review timing for your cancer and treatment intent. Safety blood tests do not by themselves show whether treatment is working.
Agree oncology/urology follow-up and the next treatment or surveillance plan.

There are no guaranteed “safe days”. Follow your own prescription and hospital instructions. This information supports a discussion; it does not authorise treatment.
Gemcitabine is drained before docetaxel is instilled. Follow your confirmed appointment and support plan.

Follow the prescribed urine, symptom and contact plan. Report fever, severe pain, bleeding or difficulty passing urine promptly. The next visit depends on safety review. Follow your confirmed appointment and support plan.
Agree the arrangements with your oncology team.

A temporary urinary catheter is used; no routine intravenous line or take-home pump is needed. Obtain written instructions for passing urine, toilet hygiene, skin exposure and sexual/contraceptive precautions.
Confirm the next treatment, tests and any scan before leaving.

Confirm the bicarbonate prescription and the fluid/diuretic plan. The source advises avoiding fluids for four hours before and until two hours after instillation, and avoiding alcohol/coffee around treatment. The team must adapt instructions for your medical conditions; do not change a prescribed diuretic yourself. The source includes prescribed sodium bicarbonate1200 mg the night before and1200 mg one hour before treatment to reduce bladder irritation. Anti-sickness medicine may be considered if nausea followed a previous instillation. Pain or spasm medicines are individual prescriptions; ask before taking ibuprofen or other medicines.
Discuss pregnancy prevention, breastfeeding, fertility concerns and product-specific sexual precautions. Your urology team confirms the written plan.
Checks help the team decide whether treatment is safe.
Follow the written plan agreed with your team.
Report new or worsening symptoms promptly.

Call your treatment team immediately for fever, shaking chills, suddenly feeling unwell, unusual bleeding, new breathlessness, very little urine, severe rash or vomiting that prevents drinking. Follow your hospital’s temperature and contact instructions. Severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, collapse or seizures: call 112/999.
Tell the nurse immediately about severe pain, bleeding, catheter difficulty or an allergic reaction. The team may postpone instillation.
Keep verified daytime and out-of-hours oncology numbers with your treatment card. The QR website is information, not an emergency service.

Published multi-centre observational evidence supports sequential gemcitabine/docetaxel as a bladder-preserving salvage option after BCG. The NCCP regimen defines the Irish doses, sequence and selected maintenance plan.

Observational results do not establish equivalence to cystectomy or other options. Published schedules differ; follow the NCCP regimen and individual urology plan, with explicit discussion of unlicensed use.

Treat selected high-risk bladder cancer when BCG has not worked, cannot be tolerated or is unsuitable. This is a bladder-preserving option for selected patients. Cystoscopy remains necessary; high-grade recurrence or progression requires discussion of other options, including bladder removal where suitable.
No. Blood counts, organ function and symptoms can make a delay or dose change safer. Your team decides whether and when to give the next dose.
Use your verified oncology daytime or out-of-hours number. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Severe symptoms require 112/999.

unique_source_inventory.text: Severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain: call emergency services. Do not wait for an online answer.

Temperature 37.5°C or higher, 36°C or lower, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell — even with a normal temperature. Call oncology immediately for fever, shaking chills, suddenly feeling unwell, unusual bleeding, new breathlessness, very little urine, severe rash or vomiting that prevents drinking. Follow your hospital’s temperature and contact instructions. Severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, collapse or seizures: call 112/999.

Follow the urgent contact instructions from your treating hospital. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Outside clinic hours, use your instructed out-of-hours pathway or the emergency department.
This page does not diagnose symptoms or decide whether it is safe to stay at home. You do not need to know which medicine caused a symptom before calling.
Help control advanced urothelial cancer using a targeted chemotherapy-carrying antibody and immune treatment.

An antibody attaches to a protein called nectin-4 and delivers a chemotherapy payload that disrupts cell division. Healthy skin, nerves and other tissues can also be affected. This is not a checkpoint immunotherapy medicine.
What to watch forReport any rash early, especially blistering, fever or mouth/eye/genital sores; also report thirst, frequent urination, numbness or new breathing symptoms.

PD-1 is a control switch on T cells, a type of immune cell. When it connects with PD-L1 or PD-L2, the T cell receives a signal to reduce its activity. Some cancers use this pathway to escape immune attack. Pembrolizumab is an antibody that blocks PD-1, helping T cells recognise and attack the cancer. It does not directly poison cancer cells like chemotherapy. Releasing this brake can also allow immune cells to attack healthy organs, which explains the different side-effect pattern and why symptoms can appear after treatment stops.

What to watch forThe immune system can also inflame healthy organs. New cough, diarrhoea, unusual weakness, severe headache, thirst or a spreading rash need prompt advice. Effects can start during treatment or after it finishes.
The drawings are simplified explanations of drug action, not anatomical pictures or a prediction of response.
This shows treatment timing, not guaranteed symptom-free days. Your team confirms the active phase and dates.

Option 1: enfortumab on days 1 and8 plus pembrolizumab200 mg on day 1, repeating every 21 days. Option 2: enfortumab on days 1,8,22 and29 plus pembrolizumab400 mg on day 1, repeating every 42 days. Your team selects one option. The six-week reference shows two enfortumab blocks; pembrolizumab day 22 applies only to option 1.
This is the NCCP 00945 advanced-disease combination. It is distinct from28-day enfortumab monotherapy and from perioperative bladder treatment.

Enfortumab is given first over 30 minutes; pembrolizumab follows over 30 minutes when both are due. Enfortumab starts at 1.25 mg/kg with a125 mg cap. Staff confirm your current dose and chosen pembrolizumab interval; pembrolizumab is not dose-reduced for toxicity.

Follow the prescribed low-risk anti-sickness plan for enfortumab. Ask about moisturiser, skin care and artificial tears. After a prior enfortumab infusion reaction, the team may prescribe antihistamine, antipyretic and intravenous steroid before later infusions. Immune effects need assessment; do not treat new diarrhoea or breathlessness as routine without contacting the team.

Cancer treatment and follow-upNCCP

These are results from the primary analysis, not a personal prognosis or a comparison with every possible treatment sequence. The current NCCP indication specifies eligibility for platinum-containing chemotherapy.
